newsitem.title: EGYPT: Human rights deteriorate in Arab world-group.
newsitem.headline: Human rights deteriorate in Arab world-group.

text.p: An Arab group said on Wednesday that human rights in the Arab world worsened in 1996 because of a "triangle of violence" caused by foreign aggression, internal conflicts and the war between governments and Moslem militants.

The Arab Organisation for Human Rights (AOHR) also slammed the use of torture by security forces that left at least 20 people dead in six countries in 1996. It criticised governments for restricting freedom of expression and political plurality.
In a special section on the rights of Palestinians, the group had harsh words for both the Israeli government and the Palestinian Authority.

"Human rights continue to deteriorate in the Arab world under the weight of the triangle of violence that is spreading in the region," said AOHR sectrary general Mohammed Fayek at a news conference to launch the report.
"This is due to foreign attacks, internal military conflicts and the confrontation between governments and political Islamic groups in nine Arab states," he added.
By foreign attacks the report referred to Israel's shelling of southern Lebanon, Turkey's incursion into northern Iraq and the U.S. bombing of military targets in southern Iraq.
Thousands of people died and hundreds more were displaced by internal conflicts in Sudan, Somalia and Iraq in 1996, it said.
Algeria topped the list of casualties from the war between governments and armed Islamic groups in 1996, but dozens died in similar conflicts in Egypt and Libya, the group added.
"Confrontations between governments and armed opposition groups have included severe violations of other principal rights," AOHR said.
"A number of Arab states have witnessed numerous detention waves, while torture scaled a high rate in interrogations or acts of revenge against political opponents," it added.

Fayek said at least 20 people died as a result of torture in Morocco, Yemen, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Algeria and the Palestinian self-rule areas. He especially criticised Israel for trying to "legalise the torture inflicted on Palestinians".
The secretary general said the organisation wanted the removal of U.N.-imposed sanctions against Libya and Iraq because they punished the people and not the governments.

In the case of Iraq, which is under sanctions for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait, AOHR said Baghdad's oil-for-food deal with the United Nations, which allowed it to sell $2 billion worth of oil to raise money to buy food and medicine for Iraqis, was an "ineffective tranquiliser".
The group said guarantees for fair trials in many Arab countries were thwarted and that governments violated freedom of opinion and expression through arrests of journalists and stricter media laws.

AOHR criticised presidential, parliamentary and local elections in several Arab countries in 1996 as exercises that "empowered the same political elite". "(This) risks multiplying political conflicts which are already sustaining factors that could lead to the explosion of the situation," it added.

The report said the rights of Palestinians suffered in 1996 by the coming to power in Israel of the right-wing Likud party, which it said "extended their oppressive measures by killing the leaders of the resistance, facing protest with increased force, killing civilians, expanding arrests, torturing detainees and closing the West Bank and Gaza".
But the group added: "It is sad to state that the autonomous regions have witnessed enormous violations by the Palestinian Authority itself."

AOHR urged the Egyptian and Libyan governments to investigate the fate of its board members and Libyan opposition figure Mansour Kikhiya, who disappeared after attending an AOHR meeting in Cairo in 1993.
